Dispersive Riemann problem for the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation

T. Congy    G. A. El    M. A. Hoefer & M. Shearer
Abstract

Long time dynamics of the smoothed step initial value problem or dispersive Riemann problem for the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (BBM) equation ut+u​ux=ux​x​tu_{t}+uu_{x}=u_{xxt} are studied using asymptotic methods and numerical simulations. The catalog of solutions of the dispersive Riemann problem for the BBM equation is much richer than for the related, integrable, Korteweg-de Vries equation ut+u​ux+ux​x​x=0.u_{t}+uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=0. The transition width of the initial smoothed step is found to significantly impact the dynamics. Narrow width gives rise to rarefaction and dispersive shock wave (DSW) solutions that are accompanied by the generation of two-phase linear wavetrains, solitary wave shedding, and expansion shocks. Both narrow and broad initial widths give rise to two-phase nonlinear wavetrains or DSW implosion and a new kind of dispersive Lax shock for symmetric data. The dispersive Lax shock is described by an approximate self-similar solution of the BBM equation whose limit as t→∞t\to\infty is a stationary, discontinuous weak solution. By introducing a slight asymmetry in the data for the dispersive Lax shock, the generation of an incoherent solitary wavetrain is observed. Further asymmetry leads to the DSW implosion regime that is effectively described by a pair of coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations. The complex interplay between nonlocality, nonlinearity and dispersion in the BBM equation underlies the rich variety of nonclassical dispersive hydrodynamic solutions to the dispersive Riemann problem.

1 Introduction

The unidirectional regularized shallow water equation, often called the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (BBM) equation [4], was originally introduced by Peregrine [41] to numerically model the development of shallow-water undular bores. The canonical representation of the BBM equation as an asymptotic model for shallow water waves has the form

ut+ux+ε⁡(u​ux−α​ux​x​t)=0,u_{t}+u_{x}+\varepsilon(uu_{x}-\alpha u_{xxt})=0, (1.1)

where ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1 and α=𝒪⁡(1)\alpha={\cal O}(1) are constants. Equation (1.1) shows that, to leading order in ε\varepsilon, ut=−uxu_{t}=-u_{x} so that (1.1) is asymptotically equivalent to the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation

ut+ux+ε⁡(u​ux+α​ux​x​x)=0.u_{t}+u_{x}+\varepsilon(uu_{x}+\alpha u_{xxx})=0. (1.2)

Despite the asymptotic equivalence of the KdV and BBM equations, their mathematical properties are drastically different. In particular, the BBM equation (1.1) yields more satisfactory short-wave behavior, owing to its regularization of the unbounded growth in the frequency, phase and group velocity values present in the linear dispersion relation for the KdV equation. This leads to a number of advantages of the BBM equation in the context of well-posedness and computational convenience. On the other hand, the BBM equation lacks integrability, which is a prominent feature of the KdV equation with many remarkable consequences including an infinite number of conserved quantities and the existence of solitons, localized solutions exhibiting elastic interactions.

In addition to the particular application of the KdV and the BBM equations as asymptotic models for weakly nonlinear shallow water waves and other dispersive media, these equations exemplify two qualitatively different ways to regularize a scalar nonlinear conservation law, acutely displayed by their normalized versions:

KdV: ut+u​ux=−ux​x​x,\displaystyle\qquad u_{t}+uu_{x}=-u_{xxx}, (1.3)
BBM: ut+u​ux=ux​x​t.\displaystyle\qquad u_{t}+uu_{x}=u_{xxt}. (1.4)

Equations (1.3) and (1.4) can be obtained from (1.2) and (1.1), respectively, by introducing the change of variables

x~=x/ε​α,t~=t/ε​α,u~=ε​u+1,\tilde{x}=x/\sqrt{\varepsilon\alpha},\quad\tilde{t}=t/\sqrt{\varepsilon\alpha},\quad\tilde{u}=\varepsilon u+1, (1.5)

and dropping the tildes.

In this paper, we study the dispersive regularization of an initial step-like transition for the BBM equation (1.4). This kind of dispersive Riemann problem was introduced and studied for the KdV equation (1.3) by Gurevich and Pitaevskii [25] using Whitham modulation theory [51]. The most prominent feature of the KdV dispersive Riemann problem is the occurrence of a dispersive shock wave (DSW), a smooth, expanding nonlinear wavetrain that replaces the discontinuous, traveling shock solution of the hyperbolic conservation law ut+(12​u2)x=0u_{t}+(\tfrac{1}{2}u^{2})_{x}=0—the Hopf equation—subject to the initial data

u⁡(x,0)={u−if ​x<0u+if ​x≥0,u(x,0)=\begin{cases}u_{-}&\text{if }x<0\\[6.0pt] u_{+}&\text{if }x\geq 0\end{cases}, (1.6)

when u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+} (the Lax entropy condition) and the shock speed cc satisfies the Rankine-Hugoniot jump condition c=12​(u−+u+)c=\tfrac{1}{2}(u_{-}+u_{+}). If u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+}, the initial discontinuity (1.6) for the Hopf equation evolves into an expanding, continuous rarefaction wave (RW), which retains its general structure under KdV dispersive regularization subject to smoothing of its weak discontinuities and small-amplitude oscillations at the left corner of the classical RW. DSWs and RWs are the only possible KdV dispersive regularizations of the Riemann problem. Because qualitatively similar DSWs and RWs have been found to arise in a variety of “KdV-like” dispersive regularizations of hyperbolic conservation laws, such DSWs and RWs are referred to as classical or convex.

It turns out that the BBM dispersive Riemann problem exhibits a number of features that are markedly different from the KdV dispersive Riemann problem, i.e., are nonclassical. To elucidate them, we first note that the consideration of discontinuous Riemann data (1.6) for a dispersive equation leads to anomalous features, such as the generation of waves with unbounded phase and group velocities in the KdV equation [6]. One way to avoid this unphysical behavior, is to introduce smoothed Riemann data, e.g.,

u⁡(x,0)=u+−u−2​tanh⁡(xξ)+u++u−2,u(x,0)=\frac{u_{+}-u_{-}}{2}\tanh\left(\frac{x}{\xi}\right)+\frac{u_{+}+u_{-}}{2}, (1.7)

where the parameter ξ\xi represents the characteristic width of the initial transition. If ξ→0\xi\to 0, (1.7) converges to the discontinuous data (1.6). For applications, the consideration of a nonlinear dispersive equation with smoothed step data of the type (1.7) constitutes a physically meaningful dispersive Riemann problem. Henceforth, we will refer to the data (1.7) as a smoothed step.

Drawing upon the theory of Riemann problems for hyperbolic conservation laws, one may hypothesize that the leading order, long-time asymptotic solution of the dispersive Riemann problem is independent of the value of ξ\xi. Indeed, the evolution of a smooth, compressive step with u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+} in the KdV equation is asymptotically described by a self-similar solution of the Whitham modulation equations, which does not involve the initial step’s width or shape and only depends on the boundary parameters u±u_{\pm} where x→±∞x\to\pm\infty [1]. However, solutions of BBM Riemann problems turn out to be quite sensitive to the value of ξ\xi, leading to qualitative differences in the wave patterns generated by the evolution of the smoothed step (1.7) with the same values of u±u_{\pm} but different values of ξ\xi. This can be understood by noting that the BBM equation (1.4) can be put in the integro-differential form [4]

ut​(x,t)=14​∫−∞+∞sgn⁡(x−y)​e−|x−y|​u​(y,t)2​𝑑y,u_{t}(x,t)=\frac{1}{4}\int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty}{\rm sgn}(x-y)e^{-|x-y|}u(y,t)^{2}dy, (1.8)

explicitly reflecting its nonevolutionary and nonlocal character. The factor e−|x−y|e^{-|x-y|} in (1.8) introduces the intrinsic BBM nonlocality length scale ℓ=1\ell=1. Consequently, the regimes of the initial value problem (1.4), (1.7) characterized by ξ≫1\xi\gg 1 and ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 are expected to be qualitatively different. The nonevolutionary character of the BBM equation also results in nonconvexity of the linear dispersion relation, with zero dispersion points for certain values of the wavenumber and background. Generally, we find that the complex interplay between nonlocality, nonlinearity and dispersion in the BBM equation gives rise to remarkably rich nonclassical dynamics that are revealed in the study of the Riemann problem.

It is worth commenting briefly on the relevance of the BBM equation (1.1) and its reduced version (1.4) for physical applications. While (1.1) is a generic asymptotic model of weakly nonlinear, dispersive waves, it is not an asymptotically resolved equation. The small parameter ϵ\epsilon cannot be scaled out of the equation while maintaining its asymptotic validity. For example, the transformation (1.5) breaks the asymptotic long wave assumption. However, there are geophysical scenarios in which the reduced BBM equation (1.4) is a reasonable physical model. An example scenario is the circular, free interface between two viscous, Stokes fluids whose long wave evolution is well-approximated by the conduit equation ut+u​ux−u​ut​x​x+ut​ux​x=0u_{t}+uu_{x}-uu_{txx}+u_{t}u_{xx}=0 [39, 34]. Other examples include a class of models for magma transport in the upper mantle ut+(un)x−(un​(u−m​ut)x)x=0u_{t}+(u^{n})_{x}-(u^{n}(u^{-m}u_{t})_{x})_{x}=0 where n∈[2,5]n\in[2,5], m∈[0,1]m\in[0,1] are parameters [43, 48] and channelized water flow beneath glaciers ut+(uα​(1−(sgn⁡(ut)​|ut​u−1|1/n)x)β)x=0u_{t}+(u^{\alpha}(1-(\mathrm{sgn}(u_{t})|u_{t}u^{-1}|^{1/n})_{x})^{\beta})_{x}=0 where n≥1n\geq 1, α>1\alpha>1, β>0\beta>0 are parameters [47]. The BBM equation (1.4) captures the quadratic hydrodynamic flux (12​u2)x\left(\frac{1}{2}u^{2}\right)_{x} and nonlocal, nonevolutionary dispersion −ux​x​t-u_{xxt} inherent to these physical models in certain parameter regimes. Therefore, the BBM equation in its reduced, normalized form (1.4) represents a significant, physically inspired dispersive regularization of the Hopf equation that is distinct from the KdV dispersive regularization (1.3).

In this paper, we report on wave structures and phenomena associated with the Riemann problem for the BBM equation. Solutions of (1.4), (1.7) include familiar wave patterns such as classical RWs and DSWs that also appear in the dispersive Riemann problem for the KdV equation. However, the BBM dispersive Riemann problem additionally exhibits a variety of nonclassical waves that do not appear as solutions to KdV-type equations. These include dynamics that depend strongly upon the smooth step transition width ξ\xi and those that do not. When ξ≪1\xi\ll 1, two-phase linear wavepackets accompany the RWs and DSWs. When u+=−u−u_{+}=-u_{-}, the BBM equation (1.4) admits a stationary, discontinuous weak solution that is stable according to the Lax entropy condition [31, 32] if 0<u−0<u_{-}. For smooth initial data (1.7) in which u+=−u−<0u_{+}=-u_{-}<0, the numerical solution evolves toward the Lax shock solution but is accompanied by increasingly short waves. These waves are described by an approximate self-similar solution to the BBM equation that we term a dispersive Lax shock. However, the solution is observed to be structurally unstable to slightly asymmetric initial conditions (u+≠−u−u_{+}\neq-u_{-}), numerically evolving into an incoherent collection of small amplitude, short waves and solitary waves. Remarkably, for u+=−u−>0u_{+}=-u_{-}>0, for which the discontinuous solution violates the Lax entropy condition and is an expansive shock wave solution of the Hopf equation, the solution of the corresponding initial value problem (1.4), (1.7) with 0<ξ≪10<\xi\ll 1 exhibits a smooth solution that approximates the discontinuity. In this case, the smooth expansion shock decays algebraically in time, giving way to a RW as shown by an asymptotic analysis in [15]. In that paper, it was also observed that when the initial data fail to be symmetric, specifically (u+≠−u−,u_{+}\neq-u_{-},), then the expansion shock may be accompanied by a train of one or more solitary waves. Finally, for arbitrary ξ>0\xi>0, we identify a regime of the BBM Riemann problem that gives rise to DSW implosion in which a nonlinear two-phase interaction develops from the small amplitude edge of the DSW. DSW implosion was previously predicted and observed in the conduit and magma equations [35].

As we have noted, the BBM equation can be viewed as a prototypical model for wave phenomena that arises in other physical systems described by nonevolutionary, nonlinear dispersive wave equations. While DSW implosion has been observed in the conduit and magma equations, other intriguing BBM wave patterns such as expansion shocks, solitary wave shedding, and dispersive Lax shocks await their realization in physical systems. These nonclassical wave patterns require new mathematical approaches for their interpretation. We utilize detailed numerical simulation, asymptotic methods, and properties of the BBM equation in order to provide a relatively complete classification of solutions of the BBM dispersive Riemann problem.

The paper is organized as follows. Owing to the classification’s richness and complexity, we begin with a high-level description of our findings in Section 2. We review the long-time asymptotic description of linear waves in Section 3 as they play a prominent role in BBM dispersive Riemann problem dynamics. This is followed by Section 4 in which rarefaction waves, dispersive Lax shocks, and expansion shocks are studied. This leads naturally to the description and analysis of the shedding of solitary waves in Section 5. Section 6 is devoted to DSW solutions, DSW implosion that includes a new two-phase description of the dynamics, and the generation of incoherent solitary wavetrains. We conclude in Section 7 with a discussion and future outlook.

2 The BBM Riemann problem: summary of solutions and analysis

With the scaling of variables,

u→α​v,x→β​X,t→γ​T,u\to\alpha v,\quad x\to\beta X,\quad t\to\gamma T, (2.1)

the BBM equation becomes:

vT+α​γβ​v​vX−1β2​vX​X​T=0.v_{T}+\frac{\alpha\gamma}{\beta}vv_{X}-\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}v_{XXT}=0. (2.2)

Thus (1.4) is invariant under the change of variables (2.1) if α​γ=β=±1\alpha\gamma=\beta=\pm 1. In particular the BBM equation remains unchanged after (u,x)→(−u,−x).(u,x)\to(-u,-x). We therefore restrict the study of the dispersive Riemann problem (1.4), (1.7) to initial data satisfying u−+u+≥0u_{-}+u_{+}\geq 0.

In this section and throughout the paper, we refer to Figures 1 and 2, which concisely capture the BBM dispersive Riemann problem classification. The figures include a partitioning of the u+≥−u−u_{+}\geq-u_{-} half plane for the smoothed step initial data (1.7) and corresponding representative numerical simulations of each qualitatively distinct wave pattern that emerges during the course of BBM (1.4) evolution. Figure 1 corresponds to the broad, slowly varying smoothed initial step in which the transition width parameter ξ≫1\xi\gg 1 (ξ=10\xi=10 in all numerical simulations). Figure 2 represents solutions for which the smoothing is narrow and sharp, corresponding to ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 (ξ=0.1\xi=0.1 in all numerical simulations). Some wave patterns persist for both large and small transition width, but many do not. We do not investigate the subtleties of the crossover ξ∼1\xi\sim 1 in which the transition width coincides with the nonlocality length, choosing instead to utilize scale separation for ξ≫1\xi\gg 1 and ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 where asymptotic methods are available.

Large transition width ξ≫1\xi\gg 1, Figure 1

When u+>max⁡(μ​u−,−u−)u_{+}>\max(\mu u_{-},-u_{-}) where μ=e−3/2/4\mu=e^{-3/2}/4, convex RWs (region aa) and DSWs (region bb) are generated, qualitatively similar to those generated by KdV (1.3) evolution. In Sec. 6.2, we use the DSW fitting approach to make quantitative predictions for the DSW’s properties (edge velocities, harmonic edge wavenumber, soliton edge amplitude, and DSW structure near the harmonic edge). We also identify the loss of convexity at the harmonic edge (where a zero linear dispersion point is attained) as the progenitor for nonclassical wave patterns when u+u_{+} is below the line μ​u−\mu u_{-}.

For initial data sufficiently close to the line u+=μ​u−u_{+}=\mu u_{-} (region cc), DSW implosion occurs. A weakly nonlinear, two-phase modulation theory using coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations is developed in Sec. 6.3, the two wave envelopes associated with modulations of short and long waves, respectively. We find that there is a spatial redistribution of energy from the long waves in a partial DSW on the right to a short wave wavepacket on the left. The partial DSW is typically accompanied by some number of depression envelope solitary waves. Very similar DSW implosion dynamics are also observed in the small transition width regime ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 (see region ff in Fig. 2).

There exists a stationary, discontinuous compressive shock solution of the BBM equation when u+=−u−<0u_{+}=-u_{-}<0 (region ee). In Sec. 4.1, we show that smoothed step initial data for this case exhibits the usual nonlinear self-steepening but is also accompanied by the continued production of shorter and shorter waves during evolution. In a neighborhood of x=0x=0, an oscillatory overshoot appears that quickly saturates to a constant magnitude. An approximate self-similar solution in the form u⁡(x,t)=g⁡(x​t)u(x,t)=g(xt) is obtained that describes these oscillations as t→∞t\to\infty. This feature is reminiscent of Gibbs’ phenomenon in the theory of Fourier series and linear dispersive partial differential equations with discontinuous initial data [7]. We refer to this wave pattern as a dispersive Lax shock. However, if the initial data is perturbed asymmetrically so that −u−<u+<σ3​(ξ)​u−-u_{-}<u_{+}<\sigma_{3}(\xi)u_{-} (region dd), then the evolution exhibits a large number of solitary waves and highly oscillatory wavepackets that do not exhibit a discernible, coherent pattern. We refer to this as the incoherent solitary wave regime and describe it in Subsection 6.4. The dispersive Lax shock and the incoherent solitary wave patterns also occur for small transition width ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 (see regions hh and gg in Fig. 2).

Small transition width ξ≪1\xi\ll 1, Figure 2

Generally, the features observed for large transition width in Fig. 1 persist into the small transition width regime shown in Fig. 2 but with modification. Rarefaction waves are accompanied by a decaying expansion shock in regions aa and bb, depression solitary waves propagating to the left in regions bb and cc, and small amplitude linear waves propagating to the left in regions cc and dd.

From the ideal expansion shock solution for symmetric data (u−=−u+<0u_{-}=-u_{+}<0) (reviewed in Sec. 4.3) into region aa for asymmetric data, a short-time analysis of the solution reveals an asymmetry that favors the generation of a depression wave for x<0x<0 (Sec. 5.2). When the threshold u+=−σ1​(ξ)​u−u_{+}=-\sigma_{1}(\xi)u_{-} is exceeded, the asymmetry produces a solitary wave that is shed from the expansion shock. Greater asymmetry generates the shedding of more depression solitary waves until u+≥0u_{+}\geq 0 and an expansion shock is no longer generated. Nevertheless, solitary wave shedding persists until u+=σ2​(ξ)​u−u_{+}=\sigma_{2}(\xi)u_{-}. Solitary Wave shedding thresholds σ1​(ξ)\sigma_{1}(\xi) and σ2​(ξ)\sigma_{2}(\xi) are analyzed in Sec. 5.3.

When u−≥0u_{-}\geq 0 (regions cc–ee), the small transition width gives rise to the generation of small amplitude wavepackets that accompany the RW or DSW. In the absence of solitary wave shedding, we can conveniently partition the initial smoothed step in the Fourier domain to prescribe initial data for the linearized BBM equation. In Sec. 3, long-time asymptotic analysis of the solution integral yields a precise prediction for three distinct wavepacket regimes corresponding to one-phase, two-phase, and Airy modulations. The analysis of DSW implosion (regions cc and ff in Figs. 1 and 2, respectively) can be viewed as a weakly nonlinear generalization of the linear wavepacket analysis.

The dynamics of DSW implosion (region ff), incoherent waves (region gg), and the dispersive Lax shock (region hh) are qualitatively similar to the respective regions in the large transition width case identified in Fig. 1.

A general conclusion from our analysis, in both the large and small transition width regimes, is that the loss of linear dispersion convexity underlies the generation of nonclassical wave patterns.

3 Linear wavetrains and Airy modulation near the zero dispersion point

In this section, we investigate the asymptotic structure of the approximately linear wavetrains generated in BBM dispersive Riemann problems with smoothed step initial data (1.7) in the parameter domain (u−,u+,ξ)(u_{-},u_{+},\xi) defined by: 0<u−0<u_{-}, μ<u+/u−<σ2​(ξ)\mu<u_{+}/u_{-}<\sigma_{2}(\xi), where μ=e−3/2/4\mu={\rm e}^{-3/2}/4 and σ2​(ξ)\sigma_{2}(\xi) is defined later in equation (5.31); see regions dd and ee in Fig. 2. The significance of σ1,2\sigma_{1,2} will be clarified later. Depending on the relative values of u−u_{-} and u+u_{+}, the initial step generates either a RW (u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+} ) or a DSW (u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+}). In both cases, an approximately linear wavetrain develops on the background u=u−u=u_{-} behind the RW or DSW and occupies an expanding region x∈[x0−​(t),x0+​(t)]x\in[x_{0}^{-}(t),x_{0}^{+}(t)], where the right boundary x0+x_{0}^{+} coincides with the trailing edge of the RW or DSW and x0−x_{0}^{-} will be determined. In this section, we use linear theory to analyze the corresponding wavetrains, hence we refer to them as “linear wavetrains”, with an understanding that this is an approximation.

3.1 Linear wavetrains in the BBM Riemann problem

We start by linearizing the BBM equation (1.4) about a constant background u¯>0\overline{u}>0, u⁡(x,t)=u¯+φ⁡(x,t)u(x,t)=\overline{u}+\varphi(x,t), |φ|≪u¯|\varphi|\ll\overline{u}, and obtain

φt+u¯​φx−φx​x​t=0.\varphi_{t}+\overline{u}\varphi_{x}-\varphi_{xxt}=0. (3.1)

For φ∝exp⁡[i⁡(k​x−ω​t)]\varphi\propto\exp[i(kx-\omega t)], we obtain the BBM linear dispersion relation:

ω=ω0​(k,u¯)=u¯​k1+k2.\omega=\omega_{0}(k,\overline{u})=\overline{u}\frac{k}{1+k^{2}}. (3.2)

Then the group velocity is given by the first derivative of ω0\omega_{0}

∂kω0=u¯​1−k2(1+k2)2,\partial_{k}\omega_{0}=\overline{u}\frac{1-k^{2}}{(1+k^{2})^{2}}, (3.3)

and the dispersion sign is defined by the sign of the second derivative

sgn⁡(∂k​kω0)=sgn⁡(u¯​2​k​(k2−3)(1+k2)3).\mathrm{sgn}\left(\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}\right)=\mathrm{sgn}\left(\overline{u}\frac{2k(k^{2}-3)}{(1+k^{2})^{3}}\right). (3.4)

The dispersion relation is nonconvex and the dispersion sign is zero for k=0k=0, k=3k=\sqrt{3} or u¯=0\overline{u}=0. We stress that it is the non-convexity of the linear dispersion relation (3.2) that gives rise to crucial differences between the BBM and KdV dispersive Riemann problems. The KdV linear dispersion relation is strictly convex for k>0k>0.

The group velocity (3.3) has a minimum when k=3k=\sqrt{3},

∂kω0≥smin​(u¯)=−u¯8,\partial_{k}\omega_{0}\geq s_{\min}(\overline{u})=-\frac{\overline{u}}{8}, (3.5)

and a maximum at k=0k=0,

∂kω0≤smax​(u¯)=u¯.\partial_{k}\omega_{0}\leq s_{\max}(\overline{u})=\overline{u}. (3.6)

Consequently, a BBM linear wavetrain that develops from a localized initial disturbance considered in isolation on the constant background u¯\overline{u} is confined to the region x∈[smin​t,smax​t]x\in[s_{\min}t,s_{\max}t] in the asymptotic regime t≫1t\gg 1, although some rapidly decaying oscillations are possible outside this region. We now place this in the context of the dispersive Riemann problem where the linear wavetrain is generated on the background u¯=u−\overline{u}=u_{-} as part of the nonlinear-dispersive regularization of smoothed step initial data. We consider two cases u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+} and u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+} separately, distinguishing between a linear wave trailing a RW or a DSW (see Fig. 2(d,e)).

(i) First, consider the case u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+} that leads to a RW. As we shall see later in Sec. 4.2, the trailing edge of the RW is located at x=u−​t=smax​(u−)​tx=u_{-}t=s_{\max}(u_{-})t. Provided u+/u−<σ2​(ξ)u_{+}/u_{-}<\sigma_{2}(\xi), no solitary wave propagates in the region x<smax​tx<s_{\max}t (cf. Sec. 4.2). Thus the two kinds of structures generated in this class of BBM dispersive Riemann problems—the linear wavetrain for x∈[smin​(u−)​t,smax​(u−)​t]x\in[s_{\min}(u_{-})t,s_{\max}(u_{-})t], and the RW for x∈[u−​t,u+​t]x\in[u_{-}t,u_{+}t]—do not overlap and can be described separately, except in the vicinity of the point x=u−​tx=u_{-}t where the two solutions could be matched. A linear wavetrain can also be generated for u+/u−≥σ2u_{+}/u_{-}\geq\sigma_{2} but we do not consider this case because one or more solitary waves may accompany the wavetrain, complicating its analysis.

(ii) For the case u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+}, which leads to a DSW, we show in Sec. 6 that the trailing edge of the DSW is located at x=s−​t<smax​(u−)​tx=s_{-}t<s_{\max}(u_{-})t so that the trailing linear wavetrain is necessarily attached to the DSW. For u+/u−>μu_{+}/u_{-}>\mu, we have smin​(u−)<s−s_{\min}(u_{-})<s_{-} and our main concern here will be the description of the linear wavetrain located outside the vicinity of the DSW trailing edge point x=s−​tx=s_{-}t, where the two modulated wavetrains could be matched.

Summarizing, we assume that for dispersive Riemann problems with μ<u+/u−<σ2​(ξ)\mu<u_{+}/u_{-}<\sigma_{2}(\xi), the generation and propagation of a small-amplitude wavetrain is governed by the linearized BBM equation (3.1) with u¯=u−\overline{u}=u_{-}, and its dynamics are fully decoupled from the nonlinear DSW or RW dynamics. In other words, we suppose that the initial profile’s Fourier spectrum can be partitioned into two essentially distinct components. The short-wave (large wavenumber) component of the spectrum is assumed to evolve according to the linear wave equation (3.1). The long-wave (small wavenumber) component of the spectrum is assumed to evolve according to the nonlinear BBM equation (1.4). Consequently, the linear wave evolution is superposed with the nonlinear evolution. We justify our partition of the initial Fourier spectrum by comparison of our linear analysis with numerical simulations. Since the Fourier transform of the initial condition (1.7) is given by the formula,

ℱ⁡[u0​(x)]=∫ℝu0​(x)​e−i​k​x​𝑑x=u+−u−2​i​π​ξsinh⁡(π​ξ​k/2)+π⁡(u++u−)​δ​(k),{\cal F}[u_{0}(x)]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}u_{0}(x)e^{-ikx}dx=\frac{u_{+}-u_{-}}{2i}\frac{\pi\xi}{\sinh(\pi\xi k/2)}+\pi(u_{+}+u_{-})\delta(k), (3.7)

the partitioning assumption implies that the Fourier transform of the linear wave φ⁡(x,t)\varphi(x,t) at t=0t=0 is approximated by

φ^0​(k)=ℱ⁡[φ⁡(x,0)]∼u+−u−2​i​π​ξsinh⁡(π​ξ​k/2),∀k∈ℝ.\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k)={\cal F}[\varphi(x,0)]\sim\displaystyle\frac{u_{+}-u_{-}}{2i}\frac{\pi\xi}{\sinh(\pi\xi k/2)},\quad\forall k\in\mathbb{R}. (3.8)

The initial condition (3.8) simplifies for a step (ξ→0\xi\to 0) to φ^0​(k)=(u+−u−)/i​k\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k)=(u_{+}-u_{-})/ik, k>k0k>k_{0}. Note that |φ^0​(k)||\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k)| is a rapidly decaying function of ξ\xi, and so no linear wavetrain is expected to be generated for ξ≫1\xi\gg 1. This agrees with Fig. 1, which shows the evolution for the dispersive Riemann problem with ξ=10\xi=10.

The solution of (3.1), is given by

φ⁡(x,t)=12​π​∫ℝφ^0​(k)​e−i​χ​(k)​t​𝑑k,χ⁡(k)=ω0​(k,u−)−k​xt,\varphi(x,t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k)e^{-i\chi(k)t}dk,\quad\chi(k)=\omega_{0}(k,u_{-})-k\frac{x}{t}, (3.9)

For notational convenience, we suppress the dependence of χ\chi on xt\frac{x}{t}.

3.2 Stationary phase analysis

Consider the asymptotic regime t→∞t\to\infty with x/tx/t fixed. We can evaluate the integral (3.9) using the stationary phase method, cf. for instance [51]. Fast oscillations average out in the integral, and the main contribution comes from the neighborhood of the stationary points knk_{n} defined as solutions of χ′​(k)=0\chi^{\prime}(k)=0, namely

∂kω0=u−​1−kn2(1+kn2)2=x/t.\partial_{k}\omega_{0}=u_{-}\frac{1-k_{n}^{2}}{(1+k_{n}^{2})^{2}}=x/t. (3.10)

A first approximation of φ⁡(x,t)\varphi(x,t) is obtained by substituting the Taylor expansions:

φ^0​(k)=φ^0​(kn)+𝒪⁡[k−kn],χ⁡(k)=χ⁡(kn)+∂k2χ⁡(kn)2​(k−kn)2+𝒪⁡[(k−kn)3].\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k)=\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{n})+{\cal O}\left[k-k_{n}\right],\quad\chi(k)=\chi(k_{n})+\frac{\partial_{k}^{2}\chi(k_{n})}{2}(k-k_{n})^{2}+{\cal O}\left[(k-k_{n})^{3}\right]. (3.11)

Equation (3.10) implies that knk_{n} depends on s≡x/ts\equiv x/t. The computation of (3.9) thus reduces to the integration of a Gaussian, and the corresponding solution φ\varphi only depends on the number of stationary points and their respective positions in kk-space:

φ(x,t)∼12​π∑nφ^0(kn)e−i​χ​(kn)​t∫ℝe−i∂k​kω0(kn,u−)(k−kn)2t/2dk.\varphi(x,t)\sim\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{n})e^{-i\chi(k_{n})t}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-i\,\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{n},u_{-})(k-k_{n})^{2}t/2}dk. (3.12)

Real solutions of (3.10) come in pairs (−kn,kn)(-k_{n},k_{n}) and, since φ^0​(−k)=φ^0∗​(k)\hat{\varphi}_{0}(-k)=\hat{\varphi}^{*}_{0}(k) and ω0​(−k,u−)=−ω0​(k,u−)\omega_{0}(-k,u_{-})=-\omega_{0}(k,u_{-}), the sum in (3.12) simplifies to [51]:

φ(x,t)∼1π∑kn>0ℜ[φ^0(kn)e−i​χ​(kn)​t∫ℝe−i∂k​kω0(kn,u−)k2t/2dk].\varphi(x,t)\sim\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{k_{n}>0}\Re\left[\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{n})e^{-i\chi(k_{n})t}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-i\,\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{n},u_{-})k^{2}t/2}dk\right]. (3.13)

The stationary phase equation (3.10) divides space-time into two regions.

(a) In the region smax>s=x/t>0s_{\rm max}>s=x/t>0, denoted hereafter as Region I, (3.10) has only one positive solution

0<k1=−u−−2​s+u−​(u−+8​s)2​s≤3,s∈(0,smax),0<k_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{-u_{-}-2s+\sqrt{u_{-}(u_{-}+8s)}}{2s}}\leq\sqrt{3},\quad s\in(0,s_{\rm max}), (3.14)

so the series (3.13) has just one term. This is comparable to what we would obtain with a convex linear dispersion relation, and we refer to this region as the convex linear regime. In fact, for k≪1k\ll 1, we obtain the linear dispersion relation ω0​(k,u¯)∼u¯​(k−k3)\omega_{0}(k,\overline{u})\sim\overline{u}(k-k^{3}), which is the linear dispersion relation for the KdV equation.

(b) In the region smin<s=x/t<0s_{\rm min}<s=x/t<0, denoted hereafter as Region II, (3.10) has k1​(s)k_{1}(s) and an additional positive solution

k2​(s)=−u−−2​s−u−​(u−+8​s)2​s≥3,s∈(smin,0),k_{2}(s)=\sqrt{\frac{-u_{-}-2s-\sqrt{u_{-}(u_{-}+8s)}}{2s}}\geq\sqrt{3},\quad s\in\left(s_{\rm min},0\right), (3.15)

so that the series (3.13) has two terms. The coexistence of two waves with wavenumbers k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} at the same position xx within Region II is a direct consequence of the nonconvexity of the dispersion relation (3.2). The modulation of the linear wave in this region dramatically differs from a convex-dispersion, KdV-type linear modulation. In Sec. 6.3 below, we show that the coexistence of two dominant wavenumbers also persists in the nonlinear regime, leading to the phenomenon of DSW implosion. The upper panel of Fig. 3 displays the comparison between the wavenumber of the waves obtained numerically from the full partial differential equation (PDE) simulation, shown in the lower panel, and the graph of xx given by (3.10) as a function of k=knk=k_{n} for a fixed value of t,t, with knk_{n}, n=1,2n=1,2 given by the formulas (3.14), (3.15). The two regions I and II are treated separately using the stationary phase approximation (3.13). A third region, denoted III in Fig. 3 and defined hereafter as x≲smin​tx\lesssim s_{\rm min}t, is resolved with an expansion near x=smin​t.x=s_{\min}t.

(Region I) In the convex linear regime of Region I, the stationary phase approximation yields

φ⁡(x,t)∼2π​ℜ⁡[φ^0​(k1)|∂k​kω0​(k1,u−)|​t​ei⁡[k1​x−ω0​(k1,u−)​t]−i​sgn​[∂k​kω0​(k1,u−)]​π/4].\varphi(x,t)\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\Re\left[\frac{\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})}{\sqrt{|\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})|t}}e^{i[k_{1}x-\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t]-i\,\mathrm{sgn}[\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})]\pi/4}\right]. (3.16)

Since arg[φ^0(k1)]=−π/2\arg[\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})]=-\pi/2 and ∂k​kω0​(k1,u−)<0\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})<0, we have

φ⁡(x,t)∼φI​(x,t)=|φ^0​(k1)|​2π​|∂k​kω0​(k1,u−)|​t​cos⁡[k1​x−ω0​(k1,u−)​t−π4].\varphi(x,t)\sim\varphi_{\rm I}(x,t)=|\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})|\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi|\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})|t}}\cos\left[k_{1}x-\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right]. (3.17)

This solution is not valid close to the so-called caustic trajectory x=u−​t=smax​t,x=u_{-}t=s_{\rm max}t, where the two dominant wavenumbers k1k_{1} and −k1-k_{1} coalesce at k1=0k_{1}=0, (cf. for instance [9]) and ∂k​kω0​(k1,u−)=0\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})=0. At this edge of Region I, one needs to consider the next order in the expansion of χ⁡(k)\chi(k) in the Taylor expansion (3.11). Besides, as pointed out earlier, a RW or a DSW develops close to the point x/t=u−x/t=u_{-} or x/t=s−<u−x/t=s_{-}<u_{-} (respectively), and the linear wave has to be asymptotically matched with the hydrodynamic state. Such a higher order derivation, which can be achieved by following the matched asymptotics procedure developed for the KdV equation [22, 33], is not important for us here because we have a well-defined initial value problem (3.1), (3.8). The comparison between the approximate solution (3.17) and the numerical solution of the dispersive Riemann problem in region I is displayed in Fig. 4.

(Region II) In Region II, for which x∈[smin​t,0]x\in[s_{\min}t,0], the modulated wave corresponding to the large wavenumber branch k2k_{2} coexists with the wave from the lower wavenumber branch k1k_{1}, leading to a modulated beating pattern. The stationary phase approximation then yields the superposition

φ⁡(x,t)∼2π​ℜ⁡[φ^0​(k1)−∂k​kω0(k1,u−)t​ei⁡[k1​x−ω0​(k1,u−)​t]+i​π/4+φ^0​(k2)∂k​kω0​(k2,u−)​t​ei⁡[k2​x−ω0​(k2,u−)​t]−i​π/4],=2π​(|φ^0​(k1)||∂k​kω0​(k1,u−)|​t​cos⁡[k1​x−ω0​(k1,u−)​t−π4]CLOSEOPEN+|φ^0​(k2)||∂k​kω0​(k2,u−)|​t​cos⁡[k2​x−ω0​(k2,u−)​t−3​π4]).\begin{split}\varphi(x,t)&\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\Re\left[\frac{\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})}{\sqrt{-\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t}}e^{i[k_{1}x-\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t]+i\pi/4}+\frac{\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{2})}{\sqrt{\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-})t}}e^{i[k_{2}x-\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-})t]-i\pi/4}\right],\\ &=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\Bigg(\frac{|\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})|}{\sqrt{|\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})|t}}\cos\left[k_{1}x-\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right]\\ &\qquad\qquad+\frac{|\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{2})|}{\sqrt{|\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-})|t}}\cos\left[k_{2}x-\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-})t-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right]\Bigg).\end{split} (3.18)

(Region III) The approximation (3.18) fails to describe the oscillations of the linear wave for x/tx/t close to smins_{\min}, corresponding to the zero dispersion point where the two branches coalesce: k1=k2=3k_{1}=k_{2}=\sqrt{3}, ∂k​kω0​(3,u−)=0\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(\sqrt{3},u_{-})=0. In this region, the expansion (3.11) is insufficient. We shall denote the union of this special region s∼smins\sim s_{\rm min} and s<smins<s_{\rm min} as s≲smins\lesssim s_{\rm min} and call it Region III. In order to describe the oscillations in this region, we expand χ⁡(k)\chi(k) close to the inflection point k=3k=\sqrt{3}

χ⁡(k)=ω0​(3,u−)−3​x/t−(x/t−smin)​(k−3)+∂k​k​kω0​(3,u−)6​t​(k−3)3+𝒪⁡[(k−3)4].\chi(k)=\omega_{0}(\sqrt{3},u_{-})-\sqrt{3}\,x/t-(x/t-s_{\rm min})(k-\sqrt{3})+\frac{\partial_{kkk}\omega_{0}(\sqrt{3},u_{-})}{6}t(k-\sqrt{3})^{3}+{\cal O}[(k-\sqrt{3})^{4}]. (3.19)

Substituting this expansion into eq. (3.9), we obtain

φ⁡(x,t)∼1π​ℜ⁡[φ^0​(3)​ei⁡[3​x−ω0​(3,u−)​t]​∫ℝei⁡(x−smin​t)​(k−3)−i​∂k​k​kω0​(3,u−)​(k−3)3​t/6​𝑑k].\varphi(x,t)\sim\frac{1}{\pi}\Re\left[\hat{\varphi}_{0}(\sqrt{3})e^{i[\sqrt{3}x-\omega_{0}(\sqrt{3},u_{-})t]}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i(x-s_{\rm min}t)(k-\sqrt{3})-i\,\partial_{kkk}\omega_{0}(\sqrt{3},u_{-})(k-\sqrt{3})^{3}t/6}dk\right]. (3.20)

With the change of variable k−3→−α​κk-\sqrt{3}\to-\alpha\kappa with α=(2/∂k​k​kω0​(3,u−)​t)1/3\alpha=(2/\partial_{kkk}\omega_{0}(\sqrt{3},u_{-})t)^{1/3}, the approximation becomes

φ⁡(x,t)=2​α​|φ^0​(3)|​Ai​[−α⁡(x−smin​t)]​cos⁡[3​(x−u−4​t)−π2],α=(323​u−​t)1/3≪1,\varphi(x,t)=2\alpha|\hat{\varphi}_{0}(\sqrt{3})|{\rm Ai}[-\alpha(x-s_{\min}t)]\cos\left[\sqrt{3}\left(x-\frac{u_{-}}{4}t\right)-\frac{\pi}{2}\right],\quad\alpha=\left(\frac{32}{3u_{-}t}\right)^{1/3}\ll 1, (3.21)

where Ai⁡(y){\rm Ai}(y) is the Airy function defined by [2]

Ai⁡(y)=12​π​∫ℝei⁡(κ​y+κ3/3)​𝑑κ∈ℝ.{\rm Ai}(y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i(\kappa y+\kappa^{3}/3)}d\kappa\in\mathbb{R}. (3.22)

The solution (3.21) represents a harmonic cosine wave modulated by the Airy function. Note that the Airy approximation (3.21) is also valid for x/t<sminx/t<s_{\min}, where the Airy modulation describes an exponential decay of the wave’s amplitude: Ai(y)∼y−1/4exp(−23y3/2){\rm Ai}(y)\sim y^{-1/4}\exp(-\tfrac{2}{3}y^{3/2}) as y→+∞y\to+\infty, which in our case translates to (x−smin​t)→−∞(x-s_{\min}t)\to-\infty.

3.3 Uniform Airy approximation

Using the technique originally developed in [8], we derive a uniform approximation that is valid in the union of regions II and III whose limiting behavior is given by (3.21) when x≲smin​tx\lesssim s_{\rm min}t and (3.18) when x≫smin​tx\gg s_{\rm min}t. We summarize here the derivation detailed in [9]. First, we suppose that the solution in region II accords with the ansatz

φ⁡(x,t)=1π​ℜ⁡[∫ℝ(ϕ0+κ​ϕ1)​ei⁡(A−κ​ζ+κ3/3)​𝑑κ],\varphi(x,t)=\frac{1}{\pi}\Re\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}}(\phi_{0}+\kappa\phi_{1})e^{i(A-\kappa\zeta+\kappa^{3}/3)}d\kappa\right], (3.23)

where ϕ0∈ℂ\phi_{0}\in\mathbb{C}, ϕ1∈ℂ\phi_{1}\in\mathbb{C}, A∈ℝA\in\mathbb{R} and ζ∈ℝ\zeta\in\mathbb{R} are functions of (x,t)(x,t) that are to be determined. By selecting the exponential’s phase ψ=A−κ​ζ+κ3/3\psi=A-\kappa\zeta+\kappa^{3}/3, we will ensure that it has the same stationary points as χ⁡(k)\chi(k) for xx close to smin​ts_{\rm min}t. Note that, although only the leading order term φ^0​(kn)\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{n}) in the Taylor expansion of φ^0​(k)\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k) near k=knk=k_{n} in the approximations leading to (3.13) and (3.20) was used, incorporating the first order term φ^0′​(kn)​(k−kn)\hat{\varphi}_{0}^{\prime}(k_{n})(k-k_{n}) in the analysis is essential for constructing a uniform approximation. We first determine the functions ϕ0\phi_{0}, ϕ1\phi_{1}, AA and ζ\zeta by evaluating the integral (3.23) using the stationary phase method. For simplicity, we consider the computation for ζ>0\zeta>0; the computation is similar in the case ζ<0\zeta<0, cf. [9]. The phase ψ\psi has two stationary points:

κ=±ζ.\kappa=\pm\sqrt{\zeta}. (3.24)

Close to the stationary points ±ζ\pm\sqrt{\zeta}, the phase is given by

ψ=A∓23​ζ3/2±ζ​(κ∓ζ)2+𝒪⁡[(κ∓ζ)3]\psi=A\mp\frac{2}{3}\zeta^{3/2}\pm\sqrt{\zeta}(\kappa\mp\sqrt{\zeta})^{2}+{\cal O}[(\kappa\mp\sqrt{\zeta})^{3}] (3.25)

Substituting the Taylor expansion of ψ\psi into (3.23), we obtain (cf. previous stationary phase computations)

φ⁡(x,t)∼1π​ℜ⁡[ϕ0+ζ​ϕ1ζ1/4​ei⁡(A−2​ζ3/2/3)+i​π/4+ϕ0−ζ​ϕ1ζ1/4​ei⁡(A+2​ζ3/2/3)−i​π/4].\varphi(x,t)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\Re\left[\frac{\phi_{0}+\sqrt{\zeta}\phi_{1}}{\zeta^{1/4}}e^{i(A-2\zeta^{3/2}/3)+i\pi/4}+\frac{\phi_{0}-\sqrt{\zeta}\phi_{1}}{\zeta^{1/4}}e^{i(A+2\zeta^{3/2}/3)-i\pi/4}\right]. (3.26)

Since the solution (3.23) should be asymptotically valid in all of region II, we impose that (3.26) identify with (3.18) for x≫smin​tx\gg s_{\rm min}t. The identification imposes

A=12[(k1+k2)x−(ω0(k1,u−)+ω0(k2,u−))t],ζ3/2=−34[(k1−k2)x−(ω0(k1,u−)−ω0(k2,u−))t],ϕ0=ζ1/4​φ^0​(k1)−2∂k​kω0(k1,u−)t+ζ1/4​φ^0​(k2)2​∂k​kω0​(k2,u−)​t,ϕ1=ζ−1/4φ^0(k1)−2∂k​kω0(k1,u−)t−ζ−1/4φ^0(k2)2​∂k​kω0​(k2,u−)​t.\begin{split}&A=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(k_{1}+k_{2})x-(\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})+\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-}))t\Big],\quad\zeta^{3/2}=-\frac{3}{4}\Big[(k_{1}-k_{2})x-(\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})-\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-}))t\Big],\\ &\phi_{0}=\frac{\zeta^{1/4}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})}{\sqrt{-2\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t}}+\frac{\zeta^{1/4}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{2})}{\sqrt{2\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-})t}},\quad\phi_{1}=\frac{\zeta^{-1/4}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{1})}{\sqrt{-2\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{1},u_{-})t}}-\frac{\zeta^{-1/4}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(k_{2})}{\sqrt{2\partial_{kk}\omega_{0}(k_{2},u_{-})t}}.\end{split} (3.27)

Then, direct integration of (3.23) yields:

φ⁡(x,t)=φuni​(x,t)=2​ℜ⁡[ei​A​(ϕ0​Ai​(−ζ)−i​ϕ1​Ai′​(−ζ))],\varphi(x,t)=\varphi_{\rm uni}(x,t)=2\Re\left[e^{iA}(\phi_{0}{\rm Ai}(-\zeta)-i\phi_{1}{\rm Ai}^{\prime}(-\zeta))\right], (3.28)

where Ai⁡(y){\rm Ai}(y) is given by (3.22) and Ai′​(y)≡d​Ai/d​y{\rm Ai}^{\prime}(y)\equiv d{\rm Ai}/dy. By construction, (3.28) is asymptotic to (3.18) when x≫smin​tx\gg s_{\rm min}t, i.e. ζ≫1\zeta\gg 1. Additionally, ϕ0∼2​α​φ^0​(3)\phi_{0}\sim 2\alpha\hat{\varphi}_{0}(\sqrt{3}), ϕ1∼−α2φ^0(3)/3\phi_{1}\sim-\alpha^{2}\hat{\varphi}_{0}(\sqrt{3})/\sqrt{3}, and ζ=−α⁡(x−smin​t)\zeta=-\alpha(x-s_{\rm min}t), such that the uniform approximation (3.28) asymptotically matches with the Airy approximation (3.21) when x∼smin​tx\sim s_{\rm min}t (recall that α≪1\alpha\ll 1 in the long time regime). Note that the uniform approximation (3.28) is also valid in the region x<smin​tx<s_{\rm min}t, or equivalently ζ<0\zeta<0, where the analytical expressions (3.14) and (3.15) are complex.

To summarize, the linear wave generated by the dispersive Riemann problem is approximated by the piecewise-defined function

φ⁡(x,t)∼{φuni​(x,t),x≤0,φI​(x,t),0<x,,t≫1,xt=𝒪⁡(1),\varphi(x,t)\sim\begin{cases}\varphi_{\rm uni}(x,t),&x\leq 0,\\ \varphi_{\rm I}(x,t),&0<x,\end{cases},\quad t\gg 1,\quad\frac{x}{t}=\mathcal{O}(1), (3.29)

where φI\varphi_{\rm I} and φuni\varphi_{\rm uni} are defined in (3.17) and (3.28), respectively. This stationary phase approximation compares well with the numerical solution, as displayed in Fig. 4.

An important consequence of the approximate initial data (3.8) for φ\varphi is that the linear wave solution φ⁡(x,t)\varphi(x,t) is valid for both polarities of the initial jump u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+} and u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+}, i.e., for either the generation of waves accompanying a RW or the generation of waves accompanying a DSW, respectively. Moreover, the linear waves accompanying a RW, φRW​(x,t)\varphi_{\rm RW}(x,t), with jump u+−u−>0u_{+}-u_{-}>0 are related to the linear waves accompanying a DSW with the same jump magnitude u−−u+>0u_{-}-u_{+}>0 by a minus sign: φDSW​(x,t)=−φRW​(x,t)\varphi_{\rm DSW}(x,t)=-\varphi_{\rm RW}(x,t). Figure 5 displays the numerical solutions for two different initial conditions u−<u+u_{-}<u_{+} and u−>u+u_{-}>u_{+} with a common difference magnitude |u+−u−||u_{+}-u_{-}|. Although the two numerical solutions are comparable, the discrepancy between them increases with increasing xx; the discrepancy is larger in Region I. In fact, the small amplitude assumption at the core of linear theory is not well-fulfilled since, initially, |φ⁡(x,0)|=𝒪⁡(|u−−u+|)|\varphi(x,0)|={\cal O}(|u_{-}-u_{+}|). It is, therefore, remarkable that linear theory still predicts the evolution of the fast oscillations with excellent accuracy, even if the small amplitude assumption is initially violated. The discrepancy in Fig. 5 is due to different matching conditions for the linear wave with the leftmost, trailing edge of the RW or DSW. This asymptotic matching has been investigated for the KdV equation in [33, 22].

Finally, we note that the asymptotic behavior (3.21) near the zero dispersion point is general and can be obtained for other wave equations exhibiting a non-convex linear dispersion relation. For example, it was obtained (with appropriate modifications due to a different form of the dispersion relation) in [49] for linear wavepackets in the Gardner-Ostrovsky equation.

4 Shocks and rarefactions

In this section, we consider shock wave and rarefaction wave solutions of the underlying conservation law ut+u​ux=0u_{t}+uu_{x}=0 and their role in the structure of solutions of the dispersive Riemann problem for the BBM equation. Stationary shocks play a significant part in this description (regions ee and hh in Figs. 1 and 2, respectively), since they are also weak solutions of the BBM equation. Of particular interest are stationary shocks that are either compressive (satisfying the Lax entropy condition) or expansive (violating the Lax condition). Stationary compressive shocks are a major feature of our analysis of dispersive Riemann problem solutions for data (u−,u+)(u_{-},u_{+}) in regions d, e of Fig. 1 and g, h of Fig. 2 while stationary expansion shocks are important in regions a and b of Fig. 2. Without loss of generality, we suppose that |u+|=1|u_{+}|=1; the solution with |u+|=b≠1|u_{+}|=b\neq 1 is given by the change of variable (x,t,u)→(x,t/b,b​u)(x,t,u)\to(x,t/b,bu).

4.1 Stationary Lax shocks

We first consider the solution when u−=−u+=1u_{-}=-u_{+}=1. Both the Hopf ut+u​ux=0u_{t}+uu_{x}=0 and the BBM equation (1.4) admit the stationary, discontinuous, weak solution

u⁡(x,t)={1x≤0−1x>0,u(x,t)=\begin{cases}1&x\leq 0\\ -1&x>0\end{cases}, (4.1)

or stationary Lax shock. The shock wave is compressive in the sense that the Hopf characteristics (with speed u±=∓1u_{\pm}=\mp 1) on each side of the shock located at x=0x=0 propagate into the shock [32]. Although this BBM solution has been acknowledged elsewhere, e.g. [15], it has remained mostly a curiosity.

We investigate the dynamics when (4.1) is smoothed at t=0t=0 according to (1.7) with u±=∓1u_{\pm}=\mp 1. The numerical solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is displayed in Fig. 6 at different times.

Evolution initially leads to the usual nonlinear self steepening (t=10t=10) due to broad initial data (ξ=10\xi=10). This long wave, Hopf equation-like evolution, is soon accompanied by oscillations (t=20t=20) when the solution is steep enough and the BBM dispersive term ux​x​tu_{xxt} is important. Dispersive regularization of shock formation typically results in a DSW (cf. Sec. 6), with an expanding collection of oscillations. The long-time dynamics of a generic DSW consists of finite amplitude waves that are bounded in wavenumber [16]. But here, oscillations of increasing, apparently unbounded wavenumber develop as time increases, concentrating near the origin. The last panel of Fig. 6 (t=300t=300) shows that the large tt behavior for both broad and narrow initial smoothed step profiles approach approximately the same structure, suggesting the existence of some self-similar asymptotic configuration. We remark that a previous numerical study of BBM has depicted similar behavior for broad, periodic initial data [21], associating it with discontinuity formation.

To further investigate these dynamics, we introduce the short space ρ=x/ϵ\rho=x/\epsilon and long time T=ϵ​tT=\epsilon t scaling where 0<ϵ≪10<\epsilon\ll 1 is a small parameter representing the characteristic length scale of the oscillations in a neighborhood of the origin. With this scaling, the BBM equation (1.4) becomes

ϵ​uT+1ϵ​u​uρ=1ϵ​uρ​ρ​T.\epsilon u_{T}+\frac{1}{\epsilon}uu_{\rho}=\frac{1}{\epsilon}u_{\rho\rho T}. (4.2)

Expanding uu in ϵ\epsilon as u=U0​(ρ,T)+ϵ​U1​(ρ,T)+⋯u=U_{0}(\rho,T)+\epsilon U_{1}(\rho,T)+\cdots, we obtain the leading order equation

U0​∂ρU0=∂ρ​ρ​TU0.U_{0}\partial_{\rho}U_{0}=\partial_{\rho\rho T}U_{0}. (4.3)

This equation can be integrated once in ρ\rho, yielding a nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation

12​U02−α=∂ρ​TU0.\frac{1}{2}U_{0}^{2}-\alpha=\partial_{\rho T}U_{0}. (4.4)

In general, α\alpha is an arbitrary function of TT. Motivated by the numerical observations in Fig. 6, we seek a self-similar solution that must be independent of the small but otherwise arbitrary parameter ϵ\epsilon, thus can only depend on ρ​T=x​t\rho T=xt:

U0​(ρ,T)=g⁡(η),η=ρ​T=x​t.U_{0}(\rho,T)=g(\eta),\quad\eta=\rho T=xt. (4.5)

In order for gg to satisfy a well-defined ordinary differential equation (ODE)

(ηg′)′+α−12g2=0,′≡dd​η,\left(\eta g^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+\alpha-\frac{1}{2}g^{2}=0,\quad^{\prime}\equiv\frac{d}{d\eta}, (4.6)

we require α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} to be constant. The boundary condition u⁡(x,t)→−1u(x,t)\to-1 as x→∞x\to\infty implies g⁡(η)→−1g(\eta)\to-1 as η→∞\eta\to\infty. Linearizing equation (4.6) about the boundary condition g⁡(η)=−1+h⁡(η)g(\eta)=-1+h(\eta) where |h|≪1|h|\ll 1, we obtain the equation

(η​h′)′+α−12+h=0.\left(\eta h^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+\alpha-\frac{1}{2}+h=0. (4.7)

If the integration constant is set to α=1/2\alpha=1/2, then h⁡(η)=0h(\eta)=0 is a stable fixed point of the homogeneous equation (4.7) with the general, Bessel-type solution h⁡(η)=C1​J0​(2​η)+C2​Y0​(2​η)h(\eta)=C_{1}J_{0}(2\sqrt{\eta})+C_{2}Y_{0}(2\sqrt{\eta}), for some C1,C2∈ℝC_{1},C_{2}\in\mathbb{R}. Consequently, the large η\eta asymptotics of the Bessel solution demonstrate that the sought solution to eq. (4.6) with α=1/2\alpha=1/2 exhibits algebraic, oscillatory decay to the requisite boundary condition

g⁡(η)∼−1+Cη1/4​cos⁡(2​η−ϕ),η→∞,g(\eta)\sim-1+\frac{C}{\eta^{1/4}}\cos\left(2\sqrt{\eta}-\phi\right),\quad\eta\to\infty, (4.8)

for some constants CC and ϕ\phi.

Since the symmetric, smoothed step initial data considered here is an odd function of xx, we seek a solution to (4.6) that is an odd function of its argument so that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0. Evaluating eq. (4.6) at η=0\eta=0 also determines g′(0)=−1/2g^{\prime}(0)=-1/2. The initial conditions

g⁡(0)=0,g′​(0)=−12,g(0)=0,\quad g^{\prime}(0)=-\frac{1}{2}, (4.9)

uniquely determine the solution of eq. (4.6) with α=1/2\alpha=1/2 that decays to −1-1 according to (4.8). We compute the numerical solution to this initial value problem and display the result in Fig. 7. Motivated by the linearized equation (4.7), we also plot in 7 the function −1+J0​(2​η−0.7)-1+J_{0}(2\sqrt{\eta}-0.7), which provides a good empirical fit to g⁡(η)g(\eta) when 2​η≳82\sqrt{\eta}\gtrsim 8. By the asymptotics of the Bessel function J0J_{0}, we can infer from Fig. 7 that C≈π−1/2C\approx\pi^{-1/2} and ϕ≈π/4+0.7\phi\approx\pi/4+0.7 in eq. (4.8).

In Fig. 8, the numerical solution of the dispersive Riemann problem for both narrow and broad initial data approaches the self-similar solution g⁡(x​t)g(xt) (with an odd extension) for large tt. The narrow case in 8(a) leads to the development of oscillations with wavelengths that are shorter than the self-similar profile whereas the broad case in 8(b) exhibits longer wavelength oscillations than g⁡(η)g(\eta). In both cases, there is no indication of discontinuity formation in finite time.

Since the odd-extended self-similar solution g⁡(η)→±1g(\eta)\to\pm 1 as η→∓∞\eta\to\mp\infty, we observe that it converges to the stationary Lax shock (4.1) as t→∞t\to\infty for each fixed xx

limt→∞g⁡(x​t)={1,x<00,x=0−1,x>0,\lim_{t\to\infty}g(xt)=\begin{cases}1,&x<0\\ 0,&x=0\\ -1,&x>0\end{cases}, (4.10)

although the convergence is not uniform in xx. The self-similar, oscillatory profile g⁡(x​t)g(xt) describes how the stationary Lax shock develops as t→∞t\to\infty. Based on these observations, we call the profile g⁡(x​t)g(xt) a dispersive Lax shock. This asymptotic solution represents a completely new type of dispersive shock structure.

The simulations in Figs. 6 and 8 exhibit behavior reminiscent of Gibbs phenomenon in the theory of Fourier series. Perhaps a more apt comparison is to initial value problems for linear dispersive PDE in which the data is discontinuous [7]. For a broad class of constant coefficient, linear dispersive PDE, the convergence of the solution as t→0+t\to 0^{+} for initial data with a discontinuity is not uniform. Moreover, it exhibits Gibbs phenomenon whereby the solution has an overshoot that, in proportionality to the jump, converges to the Wilbraham-Gibbs constant

𝔤≡1π​∫0πsin⁡zz​𝑑z−12≈0.08949.\mathfrak{g}\equiv\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{\sin{z}}{z}dz-\frac{1}{2}\approx 0.08949. (4.11)

In contrast, the dispersive Lax shock g⁡(x​t)g(xt) converges to the discontinuity (4.10) as t→∞t\to\infty. While the oscillations for η\eta sufficiently far from 00 are linear and Bessel-like, the compression of these oscillations is an inherently nonlinear process. Narrower oscillations appear as the initial smoothed step profile steepens and approaches a jump discontinuity. In contrast to the aforementioned linear initial value problems, we observe an oscillatory overshoot that can be numerically estimated from the self-similar profile g⁡(x​t)g(xt) to be, in proportion to the jump height,

maxη∈ℝ⁡g⁡(η)−12≈0.18342,\max_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{g(\eta)-1}{2}\approx 0.18342, (4.12)

a bit more than twice the Wilbraham-Gibbs constant 𝔤\mathfrak{g}.

Numerical simulations are limited by the discretization and method utilized. The structure and self-similar scaling of g⁡(x​t)g(xt) will, for large enough tt, exceed the resolution of any fixed discretization scheme. Our analysis of this dispersive Riemann problem provides a means to interpret solutions in the vicinity of dispersive Lax shocks.

We show in Sec. 6.3 that the solution of the dispersive Riemann problem for slightly asymmetric boundary conditions 0<u−+u+≪u−0<u_{-}+u_{+}\ll u_{-} is drastically different from the symmetric case investigated here. In particular, we will show that solitary waves are shedded in an incoherent fashion on top of a compressive shock structure.

4.2 Rarefaction waves

From now on, we consider the case u+=1u_{+}=1. In Fig. 9, we show numerical solutions of (1.4), (1.7) with u−<1u_{-}<1. Dispersive effects are negligible for smoothed step initial data (ξ≫1\xi\gg 1), and the asymptotic solution of the dispersive Riemann problem is a smoothed modification of the RW solution

u⁡(x,t)=uRW​(x,t)={u−,x<u−​t,x/t,u−​t≤x<t,1,t≤x,u(x,t)=u_{\rm RW}(x,t)=\begin{cases}u_{-},&x<u_{-}t,\\ x/t,&u_{-}t\leq x<t,\\ 1,&t\leq x,\end{cases} (4.13)

of the dispersionless equation ut+u​ux=0.u_{t}+uu_{x}=0. Fig. 9(b) displays good agreement between the form (4.13) and the smooth RW numerical solution of equation (1.4).

Dispersive effects are more significant for narrow smoothed step initial data (ξ≪1\xi\ll 1), as demonstrated dramatically in Fig. 9(a) and later on in Figs. 10 and 12. In the case of symmetric initial conditions u−=−1u_{-}=-1, the RW develops with an expansion shock that is described in Sec. 4.3 below. The evolution of asymmetric smoothed step initial data (having −1<u−<1-1<u_{-}<1) displays richer structure (cf. Fig. 9(a)). The interplay between long and short waves in the linear regime (clearly visible in Fig. 9(a) with OPENu−=1/2)u_{-}=1/2) is analysed in Sec. 3, and the emergence of a train of solitary waves is investigated in Sec. 5. We show in Sec. 5.2 that the development of expansion shock and solitary wavetrain structures for ξ→0\xi\to 0 is linked to the atypical early time evolution of the dispersive Riemann problem.

4.3 Expansion shocks

Consider the initial condition (1.7) with u−=−1u_{-}=-1, i.e.

u0​(x)=tanh⁡(xξ),u_{0}(x)=\tanh\left(\frac{x}{\xi}\right), (4.14)

with ξ≪1\xi\ll 1. In [15], an asymptotic solution is derived in detail, using ξ\xi as a small parameter, with long-time scaling T=ξ​tT=\xi t. Here, we outline the description in [15].

The inner structure of the solution, near x=0,x=0, is described using the same short space scaling χ=x/ξ\chi=x/\xi as that utilized for the description of the dispersive Lax shock in Sec. 4.1. However, the small parameter ξ\xi in this case is fixed by the choice of initial data (1.7). These scalings introduced into the BBM equation (1.4) lead to

ξ​uT+1ξ​u​uχ=1ξ​uχ​χ​T.\xi u_{T}+\frac{1}{\xi}uu_{\chi}=\frac{1}{\xi}u_{\chi\chi T}. (4.15)

Expanding uu in ξ\xi: u=U0​(χ,T)+ξ​U1​(χ,T)+𝒪⁡(ξ2)u=U_{0}(\chi,T)+\xi U_{1}(\chi,T)+{\cal O}(\xi^{2}), we obtain the leading order equation

U0​∂χU0=∂χ​χ​TU0.U_{0}\partial_{\chi}U_{0}=\partial_{\chi\chi T}U_{0}. (4.16)

In addition to the self-similar solution to this equation that we obtained for the dispersive Lax shock, here we obtain a separated solution describing the expansion shock. Equation (4.16) with initial condition U0​(χ,0)=tanh⁡(χ)U_{0}(\chi,0)=\tanh\left(\chi\right) corresponding to (4.14), admits the separated solution

U0​(χ,t)=11+T/2​tanh⁡χ.U_{0}(\chi,t)=\frac{1}{1+T/2}\tanh{\chi}. (4.17)

Thus the inner solution of the dispersive Riemann problem (1.4), (4.14) for ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 is given by

u⁡(x,t)=11+ξ​t/2​tanh⁡(xξ)+𝒪⁡(ξ),|x|=𝒪⁡(ξ),t=𝒪⁡(1ξ).u(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+\xi t/2}\tanh\left(\frac{x}{\xi}\right)+{\cal O}(\xi),\quad|x|=\mathcal{O}(\xi),\quad t=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\xi}\right). (4.18)

The outer structure of the solution is described using the long space scaling X=ξ​x,X=\xi x, leading to

ξ​uT+ξ​u​uX=ξ3​uX​X​T.\xi u_{T}+\xi uu_{X}=\xi^{3}u_{XXT}. (4.19)

Looking for uu in the form U~0​(X,T)+ξ​U~1​(X,T)+𝒪⁡(ξ2)\tilde{U}_{0}(X,T)+\xi\tilde{U}_{1}(X,T)+{\cal O}(\xi^{2}), we obtain the Hopf equation at leading order

∂TU~0+U~0​∂XU~0=0.\partial_{T}\tilde{U}_{0}+\tilde{U}_{0}\partial_{X}\tilde{U}_{0}=0. (4.20)

The general solution of this equation is U~0=f⁡(X−U~0​T)\tilde{U}_{0}=f(X-\tilde{U}_{0}T). The matching of U~0\tilde{U}_{0} with the inner solution (4.17), lim|X|→0U~0​(X,T)=lim|χ|→∞U0​(χ,T)\lim_{|X|\to 0}\tilde{U}_{0}(X,T)=\lim_{|\chi|\to\infty}U_{0}(\chi,T), yields

U~0​(X,T)=sgn⁡(X)+X/21+T/2.\tilde{U}_{0}(X,T)=\frac{{\rm sgn}(X)+X/2}{1+T/2}. (4.21)

This formula is continuously matched with the far-field conditions: limx→±∞u=±1\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}u=\pm 1, leading to the outer solution,

u⁡(x,t)={sgn⁡(x)+ξ​x/21+ξ​t/2,|x|<t,sgn⁡(x),|x|>t,+𝒪⁡(ξ),|x|=𝒪⁡(1ξ),t=𝒪⁡(1ξ).u(x,t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{{\rm sgn}(x)+\xi x/2}{1+\xi t/2},&|x|<t,\\[6.0pt] {\rm sgn}(x),&|x|>t,\end{cases}+{\cal O}(\xi),\quad|x|=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\xi}\right),\quad t=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\xi}\right). (4.22)

Combining the descriptions (4.18) and (4.22), we obtain the uniformly valid asymptotic solution of (1.4), (4.14) for ξ≪1\xi\ll 1

u⁡(x,t)=uexp​(x,t)=11+ξ​t/2​[tanh⁡(x/ξ)−sgn⁡(x)]+{sgn⁡(x)+ξ​x/21+ξ​t/2,|x|<t.sgn⁡(x),|x|>t.u(x,t)=u_{\rm exp}(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+\xi t/2}\big[\tanh(x/\xi)-{\rm sgn}(x)\big]+\begin{cases}\dfrac{{\rm sgn}(x)+\xi x/2}{1+\xi t/2},&|x|<t.\\[10.0pt] {\rm sgn}(x),&|x|>t.\end{cases} (4.23)

As remarked in [15], the accuracy of the asymptotic solution (4.23) is excellent, cf. Fig. 10. Note that the expansion shock structure converges to the rarefaction solution (4.13) as t→∞t\to\infty.

We also observe in Fig. 10 that the expansion shock persists for slightly asymmetric boundary conditions with −1<u−<0-1<u_{-}<0, and u+=1,u_{+}=1, see for instance the solution for u−=−0.7u_{-}=-0.7. The outer solution for such conditions is a slight modification of (4.22)

u⁡(x,t)={u−,x<u−​t+2​u−+1ξ,sgn⁡(x)+ξ​x/21+ξ​t/2,u−​t+2​u−+1ξ≤x<t,1,t≤x,|x|=𝒪⁡(1ξ),t=𝒪⁡(1ξ),u(x,t)=\begin{cases}u_{-},&x<u_{-}t+2\frac{u_{-}+1}{\xi},\\[6.0pt] \dfrac{{\rm sgn}(x)+\xi x/2}{1+\xi t/2},&u_{-}t+2\frac{u_{-}+1}{\xi}\leq x<t,\\[6.0pt] 1,&t\leq x,\end{cases}\quad|x|=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\xi}\right),\quad t=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\xi}\right), (4.24)

which is continuous at x=u−​tx=u_{-}t. Thus the truncated solution reads:

u⁡(x,t)=uaexp​(x,t)=11+ξ​t/2​[tanh⁡(x/ξ)−sgn⁡(x)]+{u−,x<u−​t+2​u−+1ξ,sgn⁡(x)+ξ​x/21+ξ​t/2,u−​t+2​u−+1ξ≤x<t,1,t≤x.u(x,t)=u_{\rm aexp}(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+\xi t/2}\big[\tanh(x/\xi)-{\rm sgn}(x)\big]+\begin{cases}u_{-},&x<u_{-}t+2\frac{u_{-}+1}{\xi},\\[6.0pt] \dfrac{{\rm sgn}(x)+\xi x/2}{1+\xi t/2},&u_{-}t+2\frac{u_{-}+1}{\xi}\leq x<t,\\[6.0pt] 1,&t\leq x.\end{cases} (4.25)

Fig. 10 shows that the asymmetric solution is in very good agreement with the numerical solution for values of u−u_{-} sufficiently close to −1-1. The absolute error between the analytical and the numerical solutions is represented in Fig. 11 for u−=−0.7u_{-}=-0.7. The largest error at t=1/ξ=10t=1/\xi=10 is approximately ξ\xi and decreases with time as expected. In the next section, we analyze the generation of solitary waves on top of the expansion shock for larger values of u−u_{-}.

5 Solitary wave shedding

In this section, we study the generation of solitary waves observed in numerical solutions. Throughout this section, we keep u+=1u_{+}=1 and consider −1<u−<1,-1<u_{-}<1, with ξ≪1\xi\ll 1 (regions a, b, c, and d in Fig. 2). Numerical results, described in Sec. 5.1, exhibit a train of solitary waves for a range of values of u−u_{-}. However, for x>0,x>0, the solutions have either a rarefaction wave accompanied by a region I linear wave (described in Sec. 3), or a portion of the expansion shock solution (described in Sec. 4.3). There are no solitary waves generated in the region x>0x>0. We can therefore restrict attention to x<0x<0.

In Sec. 5.2, we explain the appearance of solitary waves by analyzing the early time behavior of the solutions. In Sec. 5.3, we use the energy equality satisfied by smooth solutions, to establish the values of u−u_{-} for which a solitary wave is generated from those for which the solution has no solitary wave.

5.1 Numerical Solutions

We start with a qualitative description of the numerical solutions shown in Fig. 12 for various values of u−<1u_{-}<1 and fixed ξ=0.1\xi=0.1. As expected from Sec. 3, a linear wave develops to the left of the RW when u−>0u_{-}>0. Moreover, solitary waves of negative polarization are additionally generated for sufficiently small values u−<u−(2)≈0.23u_{-}<u_{-}^{(2)}\approx 0.23 of u−u_{-} as depicted in Fig. 12(a). This threshold first appears at the line L2L_{2}, u+=σ2​(ξ)​u−u_{+}=\sigma_{2}(\xi)u_{-}, of Fig. 2. The solitary wave solution of the BBM equation (1.4) is given by [40]

u⁡(x,t)=u¯+usol​(x,t,c,u¯)=u¯+3​(c−u¯)​sech2​(1−u¯c​x−c​t2),u(x,t)=\overline{u}+u_{\rm sol}(x,t;c,\overline{u})=\overline{u}+3(c-\overline{u}){\rm sech}^{2}\left(\sqrt{1-\frac{\overline{u}}{c}}\,\frac{x-ct}{2}\right), (5.1)

where cc is the wave speed and u¯\overline{u} is the background value. The wave amplitude is a=3​(c−u¯)a=3(c-\overline{u}) yielding the speed-amplitude relation

c=c⁡(a,u¯)=u¯+a/3.c=c(a,\overline{u})=\overline{u}+a/3. (5.2)

Note that the solitary wave solution exists only for c∈ℝ\[min⁡(u¯,0),max⁡(u¯,0)]c\in\mathbb{R}\backslash[\min(\overline{u},0),\max(\overline{u},0)]. The example u¯=u−=0.2\overline{u}=u_{-}=0.2 in Fig. 12(a) shows that the emitted solitary wave is locally well described by the analytical profile (5.1).

If u¯=u−=0\overline{u}=u_{-}=0, the linear dispersion relation (3.2) is ω0​(k,u¯)=0,\omega_{0}(k,\overline{u})=0, and only a train of solitary waves is generated for x<0x<0 as in Fig. 12(b). Similarly, when u−<0u_{-}<0, although a linear wave can propagate on a strictly negative background, its group velocity satisfies ∂kω0>u−\partial_{k}\omega_{0}>u_{-} so that no linear waves remain in the region x<u−​tx<u_{-}t for t≫1t\gg 1. The solitary wavetrain then propagates from the tail of the truncated expansion shock solution (4.25), as depicted in Fig. 12(b). No solitary wave emission is observed when u−<u−(1)≈−0.68u_{-}<u_{-}^{(1)}\approx-0.68. The variation of the amplitude of the leftmost solitary wave amplitude with u−∈[u−(1),u−(2)]u_{-}\in[u_{-}^{(1)},u_{-}^{(2)}] is depicted in Fig. 13.

We empirically observe that when u−∈(u(a),0]u_{-}\in(u^{\rm(a)},0] and multiple solitary waves are emitted, the amplitude a⁡(x,t)a(x,t) of the solitary wavetrain asymptotically satisfies c⁡(a,u−)=x/tc(a,u_{-})=x/t where cc is the speed-amplitude relation (5.2). A detailed study of the solitary wavetrain using, for example, Whitham modulation theory [51], is left as a subject for future work.

5.2 Early time evolution

The unusual generation of linear waves and solitary waves can be qualitatively explained by investigating the early time dynamics of the dispersive Riemann problem. We consider in this section the small-time expansion of the solution

u⁡(x,t)=u0​(x)+t​u1​(x)+𝒪⁡(t2),u(x,t)=u_{0}(x)+tu_{1}(x)+{\cal O}(t^{2}), (5.3)

where u0​(x)u_{0}(x) is given by (1.7) with u+=1u_{+}=1. Substituting (5.3) into (1.4), we obtain at the zeroth order in tt

u1′′−u1=u0​u0′,u_{1}^{\prime\prime}-u_{1}=u_{0}u_{0}^{\prime}, (5.4)

where ′≡d/dx{}^{\prime}\equiv d/dx. The small parameter condition t​u1​(x)≪u0​(x)tu_{1}(x)\ll u_{0}(x) yields the boundary conditions: limx→±∞u1​(x)=0\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}u_{1}(x)=0. Let G⁡(x)G(x) be the Green’s function satisfying,

G′′​(x)−G⁡(x)=δ⁡(x),G^{\prime\prime}(x)-G(x)=\delta(x), (5.5)

given by

G(x)=−exp(−|x|)/2.G(x)=-\exp(-|x|)/2. (5.6)

The solution of (5.4) is then

u1​(x)=∫−∞+∞G⁡(x−y)​dd​y​(u02​(y)2)​𝑑y=14​∫−∞+∞sgn⁡(x−y)​e−|x−y|​u02​(y)​𝑑y.u_{1}(x)=\int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty}G(x-y)\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{u_{0}^{2}(y)}{2}\right)dy=\frac{1}{4}\int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty}{\rm sgn}(x-y)e^{-|x-y|}u_{0}^{2}(y)dy. (5.7)

Note that u1​(x)u_{1}(x) (and higher order terms) can be directly obtained from the integro-differential form of the BBM equation (1.8) by iteration, which is part of the contraction mapping argument used to prove local existence of solutions to the BBM initial value problem [4]. The correction u1​(x)u_{1}(x) is bounded by

|u1​(x)|≤14​∫−∞+∞e−|y−x|​|dd​y​(u02​(y))|​𝑑y<1−u−2​ξ,|u_{1}(x)|\leq\frac{1}{4}\int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty}e^{-|y-x|}\left|\frac{d}{dy}\left(u_{0}^{2}(y)\right)\right|dy<\frac{1-u_{-}}{2\xi}, (5.8)

an estimate that decreases with increasing ξ,\xi, so that u1u_{1} is negligible for large ξ.\xi.
